definition: A full period of twenty-four hours comprising one complete day and one complete night; a true day reckoned from any point back to that same point, rather than from midnight to midnight.
etymology: From Greek nyx, meaning night, and hemera, meaning day. The Greeks felt the pairing needed saying explicitly, so they welded the two words together into one precise instrument. It passed into Late Latin and surfaced in English scholarly writing by the seventeenth century, mostly in medical and astronomical contexts where exactness about elapsed time could matter greatly.
usage: On the eve of Juneteenth, with the night unusually brief and the day stretched almost to its longest, the word nychthemeron feels apt — a reminder that every full turn of the clock holds both darkness and light in some proportion, and that today's proportion is tilted as far toward light as the year will allow.
